samples.text:
In modern society, many people buy more things than they really need, such as clothes, electronic devices and household items. Some people think that the government should do something to stop this behaviour. I agree with this idea to some extent.

On the one hand, buying too many goods is bad for the environment. Factories use a lot of energy and natural resources to make products, and they produce pollution. When people throw away things that they don't use, the rubbish goes to the landfill and it take many years to break down. For example, many people buy new clothes every month and wear them only few times. If the government reduce this, the environment will be more cleaner.

Also, overconsumption can cause problems for people themselves. Some people spend all their money on shopping and they have debts because of their credit cards. The government can help them by teaching about money management in schools or by controlling advertisements which make people want to buy more.

On the other hand, I think the government should not control people's life too much. People work hard and they have the right to decide how to spend their own money. Moreover, if people buy less, many shops and factories will have less customers and workers can lose their jobs. This can be bad for the economy of the country.

In my opinion, the government can encourage people to buy less by education and by making companies produce products that last longer, but it should not force people.

In conclusion, I partly agree that the government should discourage people from buying things they don't need. It can use soft methods like education, but people should still be free to make their own choices.
samples.why: Partly-agree position clear though not strongly developed · relevant ideas on both sides with general support · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · several agreement, comparative and quantifier errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
In many wealthy societies, people routinely buy clothes, gadgets and other goods that they rarely use, and some argue that governments should take steps to discourage this. I agree with this view to a large extent, as excessive consumption causes environmental and social problems that individuals alone are unlikely to solve.

The most serious consequence of overconsumption is its impact on the environment. Every product requires raw materials, energy and transport, and many items, such as cheap fashion and short-lived electronics, are thrown away after a short period. This contributes to pollution, the depletion of natural resources and overflowing landfill sites. Since these costs are not reflected in the price consumers pay, there is a strong case for government intervention to correct this.

Governments are also well placed to influence behaviour on a large scale. They could require manufacturers to make products that last longer and can be repaired, introduce taxes on goods with a high environmental impact, or restrict aggressive advertising techniques that create artificial needs. Supporting repair shops, second-hand markets and rental services would make it easier for people to consume less without feeling they are missing out.

Critics argue that such measures interfere with personal freedom and could harm economic growth, as many jobs depend on consumer spending. These concerns are valid, and governments should avoid telling people what they may or may not buy. However, encouraging more sustainable habits does not mean banning shopping; it means shifting the economy towards durable goods and services, which can also creates employment, for example in repair and recycling.

In conclusion, I believe governments should discourage people from buying more than they need, mainly by encouraging durability, reducing waste and regulating advertising. Such measures can protect the environment while still respecting individual choice.

samples.text:
Consumer culture in many prosperous countries encourages people to buy far more than they need, from fast fashion to frequently upgraded phones. The suggestion that governments should actively discourage this behaviour raises questions about both sustainability and personal freedom. On balance, I agree that intervention is justified, provided it targets the systems that drive overconsumption rather than policing individual purchases.

The environmental argument is compelling. The production, shipping and disposal of consumer goods account for a considerable share of resource use and emissions, and the problem is aggravated by products designed to be replaced rather than repaired. A garment worn a handful of times before being discarded, or a device abandoned because a single component has failed, represents a significant waste of materials and energy. Because these environmental costs are largely borne by society rather than by the buyer, the market alone has little incentive to correct them.

Governments possess tools that individuals do not. Legislation requiring durability, access to spare parts and a right to repair would extend the life of countless products. Tax policy could make repair and second-hand goods cheaper relative to new ones, while tighter rules on advertising, particularly the targeted online promotions that exploit impulse buying, would reduce the constant pressure to acquire more. Measures of this kind reshape the choices available without dictating what anyone must buy.

The main objections are that such policies infringe personal liberty and threaten economic growth. The first is less persuasive when intervention focuses on product standards and marketing rather than consumer decisions. The second deserves more attention, since many jobs depend on retail spending, but a shift towards repair, refurbishment and services can generate employment of its own.

In conclusion, governments are right to discourage excessive consumption, though the most effective and legitimate way to do so is by changing how goods are made and marketed, rather than by restricting what people are allowed to buy.
samples.why: Clear, well-qualified position throughout · ideas extended with precise examples · objections evaluated rather than merely listed · skilful cohesion · wide, natural vocabulary · accurate, varied complex structures.
